title: Paired passages: agreement, disagreement, shared assumptions
blurb: Read two authors on one topic and pin down where they agree, where they split, what both take for granted and how one would answer the other.
question: A pediatrician argues for a city tax on sugary drinks. A store owner agrees children drink too much sugar but says the tax would hurt low-income families. A TEAS item asks what the two authors disagree about. One option says 'whether children consume too much sugar.' Why is that wrong?

teach.body: Formally, paired passages are two texts on the same topic, usually by different authors, that you must compare (find similarities) and contrast (find differences). Items ask about the shared topic, a point of agreement, a point of disagreement, a shared assumption, a difference in purpose, audience or genre, and how one author would respond to the other. In plain English: figure out each author's position first, then map how the two positions line up.

Passage 1 (pediatrician): Children in our city drink far too much sugar, and I see the results in my clinic every day. A two-cent-per-ounce tax on sugary drinks would push families toward water and milk, and the money could fund healthy school lunches.

Passage 2 (store owner): No one disputes that kids consume too much sugar. But a drink tax falls hardest on low-income families and on small shops like mine. Teaching nutrition in schools would cut sugar intake without punishing anyone's budget.

teach.h: Reading a pair in four moves
items: Sum up Passage 1's position in a few words: 'Tax sugary drinks.'
Sum up Passage 2's position: 'Too much sugar, but no tax; teach nutrition.'
Label the relationship: they agree on the problem and disagree on the solution.
Test every option against BOTH passages, and check each detail comes from the passage the question names.

teach.body: A shared assumption is a belief both authors take for granted without arguing for it. Both sugar-tax authors assume that lowering children's sugar intake is worth doing; neither stops to prove it. Test an option by asking: would each author's argument fall apart if this were false? If yes for both, it is a shared assumption. A point of agreement, by contrast, is something both authors actually state.

teach.caption: The right response uses the second author's own stated reasons, not reasons you invent.

teach.text: Paired-passage traps: a detail from the wrong passage, an option true of one passage when the question asks about both, a minor shared detail chosen over the central idea, and 'they disagree' chosen because one author is emotional and the other is calm. Different tone is not disagreement.

teach.h: Scenario: Luis answers a disagreement item
teach.body: Luis Hernandez, applying to a respiratory therapy program, is asked what the two authors disagree about. He rejects 'whether children consume too much sugar' because the store owner says no one disputes it: that is agreement. He rejects 'whether school lunches are healthy' because Passage 2 never discusses lunches. He chooses 'whether a tax is the best way to reduce sugar intake', the one point where their positions split.

items: Find each author's position before reading the options.
Agreement and disagreement are stated; a shared assumption is unstated.
An option for 'both' must fit both passages.
A 'how would Author 2 respond' answer uses Author 2's own reasons.
Different tone or genre does not mean the authors disagree.

summary: You can now map two passages on the same topic: where the authors agree, where they disagree, what they both assume and how their purposes differ. You can also predict how one author would respond to the other using that author's own reasons.

A.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: Young children gain little from homework. Studies of elementary students find almost no link between homework time and test scores. Their evenings are better spent reading for fun, playing outside and sleeping.

Passage 2: A short homework assignment, no more than twenty minutes, teaches young children to manage time and take responsibility. Hours of worksheets, though, only make children dread school.

On which point would both authors most likely agree?
options: Homework is the best way to build responsibility.
Young children should not be given homework.
Long homework loads do not help young children.
Test scores rise when children do more homework.
A.why: Passage 1 says homework gives young children little benefit, and Passage 2 warns that hours of worksheets make children dread school. Both would reject heavy homework loads for young children.

whyNot.0: This is Passage 2's view only, and even Passage 2 does not call homework the best way.
whyNot.1: Passage 2 supports short assignments, so it would not agree to no homework.
whyNot.3: Passage 1 says studies find almost no such link, and Passage 2 does not claim it.

A.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: Telehealth has changed life for my rural patients. A mother who once drove two hours each way for her son's asthma check-ups now meets the doctor by video in fifteen minutes.

Passage 2: Video visits are convenient, but a camera cannot listen to lungs or feel a swollen gland. Telehealth should support in-person care, not replace it.

How would the author of Passage 2 most likely respond to Passage 1?
options: By urging rural clinics to stop offering any video visits
By noting that some asthma checks need an in-person exam
By arguing that the two-hour drive cost the family little
By agreeing that video visits can replace all check-ups
A.why: Author 2 accepts that telehealth is convenient but says a camera cannot listen to lungs. Applied to an asthma check-up, that reason leads to pointing out the need for in-person exams.

whyNot.0: Author 2 calls video visits convenient and wants them to support care, not to stop.
whyNot.2: Author 2 calls video visits convenient, so Author 2 grants that saving the two-hour drive matters.
whyNot.3: Author 2 says telehealth should not replace in-person care.

A.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: The stretch of Elm Street outside Hillcrest Elementary needs a signaled crosswalk. Children dart across four lanes to reach the school's side door.

Passage 2: Speed bumps on Elm Street would slow drivers near the school far more cheaply than a new signal, and they would work at every hour, not just when the light is red.

Which assumption do both authors share?
options: Traffic on Elm Street is a danger to people on foot near the school.
Speed bumps cost the city less to install than a crosswalk signal.
Children should be taught to use the main door instead of the side.
The school should move its side door away from the busy street.
A.why: Both proposals exist to protect people crossing near the school. Neither author argues that the street is dangerous; both take it for granted, which makes it a shared assumption.

whyNot.1: This is Passage 2's claim; Passage 1 never discusses cost.
whyNot.2: Neither author proposes changing which door children use.
whyNot.3: Neither author suggests moving the door; both focus on the street.

B.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: Daylight saving time began in the United States during World War I as a way to save fuel. It was dropped after the war, revived in World War II and set into national law in 1966.

Passage 2: It is time to stop changing our clocks twice a year. The spring switch costs us an hour of sleep, and drowsy drivers pay the price. Congress should pick one time and keep it.

How do the purposes of the two passages differ?
options: Passage 1 argues for clock changes; Passage 2 argues against them.
Passage 1 describes sleep loss; Passage 2 describes wartime fuel use.
Passage 1 entertains with a story; Passage 2 informs with statistics.
Passage 1 explains a history; Passage 2 argues for ending a practice.
B.why: Passage 1 gives a neutral history of daylight saving time, so its purpose is to inform. Passage 2 states a position and calls on Congress to act, so its purpose is to persuade.

whyNot.0: Passage 1 takes no side; it reports dates and events.
whyNot.1: This swaps the content: Passage 1 covers fuel and wars, Passage 2 covers sleep.
whyNot.2: Passage 1 is factual history, and Passage 2 gives no statistics.

B.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: Ending library late fines brings families back. After Clearwater dropped its fines, the number of active child library cards rose by 18 percent in a year.

Passage 2: Fines remind borrowers that a library book belongs to everyone. The small sums also helped our branch buy new books each year.

Which detail from Passage 2 supports its author's position?
options: Fine money once helped the branch buy new books.
Child library cards rose by 18 percent in a year.
Families returned after the fines were dropped.
Clearwater's library dropped its fines last year.
B.why: Passage 2 defends fines, and its own detail that fine money paid for new books supports that position.

whyNot.1: This detail comes from Passage 1 and supports the opposite position.
whyNot.2: This is Passage 1's claim, used to argue against fines.
whyNot.3: This background detail is from Passage 1, not Passage 2.

B.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: Hospitals should allow family visits at any hour. Patients with loved ones nearby feel less anxious and often follow their care plans more closely.

Passage 2: As a night-shift nurse, I welcome families. But visitors arriving at 2 a.m. wake roommates and interrupt care. Open visiting works best with quiet-hour rules.

What is the main point of disagreement between the authors?
options: Whether family visits benefit hospital patients
Whether nurses should welcome patients' families
Whether visiting should be limited at night
Whether patients follow their care plans at home
B.why: Author 1 wants visits at any hour; Author 2 wants quiet-hour rules at night. That is where their positions split.

whyNot.0: Both authors accept that family presence helps; Author 2 says she welcomes families.
whyNot.1: Author 2 says she welcomes families, and Author 1 does not discuss nurses.
whyNot.3: Neither passage discusses care at home.

C.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: I'm furious that our county still has no needle-free flu vaccine option for kids. Every fall, my six-year-old screams through his shot, and some parents I know skip it entirely to avoid the scene.

Passage 2: County health data show that about one in five parents of young children delay flu vaccination because of their child's fear of needles. A nasal spray option could raise vaccination rates.

Which statement best describes the relationship between the passages?
options: They disagree, because Passage 1 is angry and Passage 2 is calm.
They agree that needle fear can delay children's vaccinations.
Passage 2 disproves Passage 1's claim about parents skipping shots.
Passage 1 opposes flu vaccines; Passage 2 supports flu vaccines.
C.why: Passage 1 describes parents skipping shots to avoid a child's fear; Passage 2's data show needle fear delays vaccination. Different tones, same point.

whyNot.0: A difference in tone is not a disagreement; their claims line up.
whyNot.2: Passage 2's data support Passage 1's observation rather than disproving it.
whyNot.3: Passage 1 wants a needle-free option, not fewer vaccines; it does not oppose vaccination.

C.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: Nursing programs should require applicants to complete 40 volunteer hours in a health setting. Seeing patient care up close helps applicants decide whether nursing truly suits them.

Passage 2: A volunteer-hour requirement favors applicants who can afford unpaid time. Many strong candidates work two jobs. Programs should accept paid work in health care, such as a job as a nursing aide, in place of volunteering.

Which assumption do the two authors share?
options: Volunteer hours are the fairest test of an applicant.
Most nursing applicants already work in health care.
Paid work teaches more than volunteering in a clinic.
Health-setting experience is useful to applicants.
C.why: Author 1 wants volunteer experience in a health setting; Author 2 wants paid health-care work to count instead. Both take for granted that health-setting experience is valuable to applicants.

whyNot.0: Author 2 argues the requirement is unfair, so this is not shared.
whyNot.1: Author 2 says many candidates work, but neither says most work in health care.
whyNot.2: Author 2 wants paid work accepted as an equal, not claimed to be better.

C.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: Standing desks cut sitting time. In one office study, workers given standing desks sat about an hour less each day after three months.

Passage 2: Standing still for long periods strains the legs and back. Workers do best when they change position often, sitting, standing and walking through the day.

Which statement would the author of Passage 2 most likely make about the study in Passage 1?
options: Sitting an hour less each day proves standing desks improve health.
Less sitting is helpful only if workers do not stand still too long.
The study shows that workers should stand for their whole workday.
Office workers should go back to sitting at regular desks all day.
C.why: Author 2's own reasons are that standing still strains the body and that changing position is best. Applied to the study, Author 2 would accept less sitting as useful but warn against long periods of standing.

whyNot.0: Author 2 warns about the strain of standing and would not call this proof of better health.
whyNot.2: Standing all day contradicts Author 2's advice to change position often.
whyNot.3: Author 2 recommends mixing positions, not sitting all day.

reteach.title: Think of two friends picking a restaurant
reteach.question: Nia wants tacos; Sam wants pizza. Both are starving and both want to eat nearby. Where do they agree, where do they disagree, and what are they both assuming?

blocks.body: Nia and Sam agree they are hungry and want somewhere close: both say so. They disagree about what to eat. And they both assume, without saying it, that they will eat together tonight; neither argues for that. Paired passages work the same way: stated common ground is agreement, the split is disagreement, and the unspoken starting point both rely on is the shared assumption.

blocks.text: If Sam is grumpy and Nia is cheerful, that does not change what they agree on. Tone is not position.

explain.body: A point of agreement is something both authors state or clearly accept. It is often the problem itself: two authors can agree a problem exists while proposing different fixes.

test.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: Our town's playgrounds are crumbling. A bond measure would fund repairs within two years.

Passage 2: The playgrounds clearly need work, but a bond adds debt. Local businesses could sponsor repairs instead.

On which point do the authors agree?
options: The town should take on debt for repairs.
Local businesses should pay for the work.
The town's playgrounds need to be repaired.
Repairs should be finished within two years.
test.why: Passage 1 says the playgrounds are crumbling; Passage 2 says they clearly need work. Both agree on the problem.

whyNot.0: Passage 2 objects to the bond because it adds debt.
whyNot.1: This is Passage 2's proposal; Passage 1 favors a bond.
whyNot.3: The two-year timeline appears only in Passage 1.

explain.body: Disagreement is where the authors' positions split. Find each author's claim, then name the single issue on which they take opposite sides. Do not confuse a difference in tone or topic emphasis with a disagreement.

test.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: Hospital cafeterias should remove fried foods. Staff and visitors need healthy choices, and the hospital should set an example.

Passage 2: Hospital cafeterias should add more healthy choices, but adults can decide for themselves. Removing fried foods would just send people to the fast-food place across the street.

What do the authors disagree about?
options: Whether healthy food should be offered
Whether fried foods should be removed
Whether fried foods are a healthy choice
Whether staff need healthy choices
test.why: Author 1 wants fried foods removed; Author 2 opposes removal. Both support healthy options.

whyNot.0: Both authors want healthy food offered.
whyNot.2: Neither author defends fried foods as healthy; Author 2 objects to removing them, not to calling them unhealthy.
whyNot.3: Author 2 also wants more healthy choices, so this is not in dispute.

explain.body: A shared assumption is never argued for: both authors simply rely on it. Ask: if this were false, would BOTH arguments collapse? If yes, it is shared.

test.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: The clinic should hire a second interpreter so Spanish-speaking patients wait less.

Passage 2: The clinic should use a phone interpreter service, which costs less and covers many languages.

Which assumption do both authors share?
options: Phone services are cheaper than hiring staff.
Most of the clinic's patients speak Spanish.
A second interpreter would shorten wait times.
Some patients need language help at visits.
test.why: Both proposals exist only because patients need language help at the clinic. Neither author argues for that need; both take it for granted.

whyNot.0: This is Passage 2's claim, not shared by Passage 1.
whyNot.1: Neither passage says most patients speak Spanish, and Passage 2 mentions many languages.
whyNot.2: This is Passage 1's claim; Passage 2 proposes a different solution.

explain.body: Two authors may write for different purposes (one informs, one persuades) or in different genres. When asked how one author would respond to the other, apply that author's own stated reasons to the other's claim.

test.q:
Read the two passages.

Passage 1: Four-day school weeks save districts money on buses and heating.

Passage 2: When my district moved to four days, working parents like me had to pay for a fifth day of child care every week.

How would the author of Passage 2 most likely respond to Passage 1?
options: District savings shift costs onto working families.
Bus and heating costs are lower in a four-day week.
Districts should cut bus routes to save more money.
Students learn more in a four-day school week.
test.why: Author 2's own experience is paying for an extra day of child care. Applied to Passage 1's savings claim, Author 2 would say the savings move costs onto families.

whyNot.1: This restates Passage 1's claim rather than responding to it from Author 2's view.
